Quasiconvexity for the Dacorogna–Marcellini Energy

Giuseppe Bruno Affiliation: University of Bern and Google DeepMind    Federico Pasqualotto Affiliation: University of California San Diego and Google DeepMind
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove that the planar Dacorogna–Marcellini energy fγ​(A)=|A|4−2​γ​|A|2​detAf_{\gamma}(A)=|A|^{4}-2\gamma|A|^{2}\det A is quasiconvex exactly when it is rank-one convex, i.e. if and only if |γ|≤23|\gamma|\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}. The proof uses a monotonicity property of the energy functional along the componentwise heat flow. As a corollary of our method, we show that for homogeneous quartic polynomials on 2×22\times 2 matrices invariant by left and right rotation, quasiconvexity is equivalent to rank one convexity.

1 Introduction

Let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a bounded domain and consider a first-order variational integral

ℐf​(u)=∫Ωf⁡(D​u​(x))​𝑑x,u:Ω→ℝm,\mathcal{I}_{f}(u)=\int_{\Omega}f(Du(x))\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{m},

where f:ℝm×n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R} is continuous. In the direct method of the calculus of variations, weak lower semicontinuity of ℐf\mathcal{I}_{f} allows one to pass to the weak limit of a minimizing sequence and is therefore a fundamental property in existence results [5]. For scalar problems, ordinary convexity gives the relevant condition, whereas for vector-valued maps the situation is more difficult.

Morrey introduced quasiconvexity in his study of this question [19]. An integrand f:ℝm×n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R} is quasiconvex if

∫Uf⁡(F+D​φ)​𝑑x≥|U|​f​(F)\int_{U}f(F+D\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}x\geq|U|f(F) (1.1)

for every bounded Lipschitz domain U⊂ℝnU\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, every F∈ℝm×nF\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, and every φ∈W01,∞​(U,ℝm)\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_{0}(U,\mathbb{R}^{m}). When m=1m=1 or n=1n=1, this condition is equivalent to convexity, whereas for m,n≥2m,n\geq 2 it is much harder to check.

Since the definition is global in the perturbation φ\varphi, quasiconvexity is difficult to verify directly. Rank-one convexity provides a simpler necessary condition: the integrand ff is rank-one convex if

f⁡((1−t)​A+t​B)≤(1−t)​f​(A)+t​f​(B)f\bigl((1-t)A+tB\bigr)\leq(1-t)f(A)+tf(B)

whenever t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], A,B∈ℝm×nA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, and rank⁡(A−B)≤1\operatorname{rank}(A-B)\leq 1. For a twice differentiable integrand, this is equivalent to the Legendre–Hadamard inequalities

D2​f​(A)​[a⊗b,a⊗b]≥0,a∈ℝm,b∈ℝn.D^{2}f(A)[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]\geq 0,\qquad a\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\quad b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. (1.2)

Every quasiconvex integrand is rank-one convex, and the question of whether the converse holds is known as Morrey’s problem.

Polyconvexity provides a useful sufficient condition: an integrand is polyconvex if it is a convex function of all the minors of its matrix argument. In dimension 2×22\times 2, this means that

f⁡(A)=g⁡(A,detA)f(A)=g(A,\det A)

for some convex function g:ℝ2×2×ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, a condition introduced by Ball in nonlinear elasticity [4]. Together, these notions satisfy

convex⟹polyconvex⟹quasiconvex⟹rank-one convex.\text{convex}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{polyconvex}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{quasiconvex}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{rank-one convex}.

Although none of the reverse implications holds in full generality, the last one is the most relevant here. Šverák constructed a rank-one-convex integrand on ℝ3×2\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2} which is not quasiconvex [21]. This settled the question in higher target dimension, but the construction does not descend to ℝ2×2\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, which became the basic testing ground for the gap between rank-one convexity and quasiconvexity.

The planar problem has also been studied by imposing additional structure on the matrices or on the integrand. Müller proved that rank-one convexity implies quasiconvexity on diagonal matrices [20], and Harris, Kirchheim, and Lin extended this result to upper-triangular 2×22\times 2 matrices [15]. Székelyhidi described the geometry of rank-one-convex hulls in ℝ2×2\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} and of quasiconvex hulls in the symmetric subspace [22, 23]. Faraco and Székelyhidi proved a localization theorem for quasiconvex hulls in ℝ2×2\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, while Kirchheim and Székelyhidi obtained a characterization of incompatible sets of planar gradients [11, 16]. For rotationally invariant integrands, Dacorogna and Koshigoe showed that convexity and polyconvexity can be tested on diagonal matrices, although the same reduction is not valid for rank-one convexity and quasiconvexity [8]. A stronger conclusion holds in the isochoric class from nonlinear elasticity, where Martin, Ghiba, and Neff proved that every objective and isotropic rank-one-convex energy on GL+​(2)\mathrm{GL}^{+}(2) is polyconvex [17].

Connections with quasiconformal mapping theory are organized around the Burkholder integrands. Astala, Iwaniec, Prause, and Saksman proved sharp quasiconcavity inequalities for these integrands under a pointwise distortion restriction [3]. Guerra and Kristensen later obtained automatic polyconvexity and conditional quasiconvexity results for nonnegative homogeneous isotropic rank-one-convex integrands [13]. More recently, Astala, Faraco, Guerra, Koski, and Kristensen proved quasiconvexity of the local Burkholder functional and obtained quasiconvex energies on the set of matrices with positive determinant which are not polyconvex [2].

Finite elasticity provides another planar candidate family. For objective and isotropic energies with an additive volumetric–isochoric split, Voss, Martin, Ghiba, and Neff reduced part of Morrey’s problem to the quasiconvexity of the rank-one-convex energy Wmagic+W_{\mathrm{magic}}^{+} [24]. Numerical tests based on finite elements, derivative-free optimization, and neural networks did not find a violation of quasiconvexity for this energy [25].

The Dacorogna–Marcellini family was introduced to study this planar gap. For γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}, it is given by

fγ​(A)=|A|4−2​γ​|A|2​detA,A∈ℝ2×2,f_{\gamma}(A)=|A|^{4}-2\gamma|A|^{2}\det A,\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, (1.3)

where |A||A| is the Frobenius norm. Dacorogna and Marcellini introduced this quartic family in [9]. Its local convexity conditions can be computed exactly, while part of the family lies beyond the polyconvex range, which makes it a useful model for the planar problem.

The analysis of Dacorogna, Douchet, Gangbo, and Rappaz and of Alibert and Dacorogna [6, 1] showed that

fγ​ is convex\displaystyle f_{\gamma}\text{ is convex} ⟺|γ|≤2​23,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\quad|\gamma|\leq\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3},
fγ​ is polyconvex\displaystyle f_{\gamma}\text{ is polyconvex} ⟺|γ|≤1,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\quad|\gamma|\leq 1,
fγ​ is rank-one convex\displaystyle f_{\gamma}\text{ is rank-one convex} ⟺|γ|≤23.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\quad|\gamma|\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.

The endpoint |γ|=2/3|\gamma|=2/\sqrt{3} is rank-one convex but not polyconvex, while polyconvexity proves quasiconvexity only for |γ|≤1|\gamma|\leq 1. This leaves the interval

1<|γ|≤231<|\gamma|\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}

open. Failure of quasiconvexity in this interval would provide a counterexample to the planar implication, while validity up to the endpoint would make the quasiconvexity and rank-one-convexity thresholds coincide for the whole family.

The first investigations were numerical, and Dacorogna, Douchet, Gangbo, and Rappaz found evidence for quasiconvexity at the endpoint [6]. Alibert and Dacorogna then proved that there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that

|γ|≤1+ε⟹fγ​ is quasiconvex,|\gamma|\leq 1+\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_{\gamma}\text{ is quasiconvex},

and hence obtained an explicit quasiconvex integrand which is not polyconvex [1]. Their argument crossed the polyconvex threshold but did not reach the full rank-one-convexity range, so the remaining gap continued to be studied numerically. Gremaud used a simulated-annealing method, while Dacorogna and Haeberly compared several numerical schemes, and both studies found evidence that quasiconvexity persists throughout the rank-one-convex range [12, 7]. Gutiérrez and Villavicencio studied a broader optimization problem for quartic polynomials without finding a planar counterexample [14]. Dong and Enakoutsa later reported numerical violations for the Dacorogna–Marcellini family [10]. The different outcomes did not determine the quasiconvexity threshold.

Theorem 1.

For |γ|≤2/3|\gamma|\leq 2/\sqrt{3}, the function fγf_{\gamma} defined in (1.3) is quasiconvex.

Since quasiconvexity implies rank-one convexity, the known obstruction beyond 2/32/\sqrt{3} is also necessary. Thus

fγ is quasiconvex⟺fγ is rank-one convex⟺|γ|≤23.f_{\gamma}\text{ is quasiconvex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_{\gamma}\text{ is rank-one convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad|\gamma|\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.

In particular, the whole interval 1<|γ|≤2/31<|\gamma|\leq 2/\sqrt{3} consists of quasiconvex integrands which are not polyconvex.

Our method also applied to more general invariant quartic homogeneous polynomials.

Theorem 2.

Let Q:ℝ2×2→ℝQ:\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\to\mathbb{R} be a homogeneous polynomial of degree 4 such that

Q⁡(U​F​VT)=Q⁡(F)for every ​F∈ℝ2×2​ and ​U,V∈S​O​(2).Q(UFV^{T})=Q(F)\qquad\text{for every }F\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\text{ and }U,V\in SO(2).

Then QQ is quasiconvex if and only if it is rank-one convex.

The proof of Theorem 2 proceeds in the same way as the proof of Theorem 1, once one observes that every such polynomial admits a unique representation

Q⁡(F)=a​|F|4+b​|F|2​detF+c​(detF)2.Q(F)=a|F|^{4}+b|F|^{2}\det F+c(\det F)^{2}.

for a,b,c∈ℝa,b,c\in\mathbb{R}.

Proof strategy.

The proof uses a monotonicity argument rather than a direct estimate of (1.1). Given a compactly supported perturbation φ\varphi, we evolve it by the heat equation

φτ=eτ​Δ​φ.\varphi_{\tau}=e^{\tau\Delta}\varphi.

As τ→∞\tau\to\infty, the perturbation disappears, and differentiation of the relative energy along this path reduces the proof to the integrated second-variation inequality

∫ℝ2∑i=12D2​fγ​(D​v)​[∂iD​v,∂iD​v],𝑑x≥0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{2}D^{2}f_{\gamma}(Dv)[\partial_{i}Dv,\partial_{i}Dv],\mathrm{d}x\geq 0.

This step is related to the flow-interchange method of Matthes, McCann, and Savaré [18], since the functional is studied along an auxiliary flow with simple long-time behavior.

Since the second-variation density need not be pointwise nonnegative, we construct an S​O​(2)×S​O​(2)SO(2)\times SO(2)-invariant exact two-form ωγ=d​αγ\omega_{\gamma}=\mathrm{d}\alpha_{\gamma} on matrix space. Its pullback by a gradient has zero integral,

∫ℝ2(D​v)∗​ωγ=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(Dv)^{*}\omega_{\gamma}=0.

We choose ωγ\omega_{\gamma} so that adding it to the second-variation density makes the resulting expression pointwise nonnegative, thereby changing the density without changing its integral.

The rotational invariance of both the energy and the correction reduces the pointwise inequality to matrices of the form diag⁡(1,ρ)\operatorname{diag}(1,\rho). At the endpoint |γ|=2/3|\gamma|=2/\sqrt{3}, it remains to prove that an explicit quadratic form is nonnegative, while the intermediate values of γ\gamma follow by interpolation. The next section develops the heat-flow criterion, and the final section constructs the exact correction and verifies the pointwise inequality.

2 Monotonicity under heat flow

To study the functional generated by fγf_{\gamma}, we use a strategy related to the flow-interchange technique of Matthes, McCann, and Savaré from Wasserstein gradient flow theory [18]. The idea is to compute the evolution of a functional along an auxiliary flow rather than along its own gradient flow. Here, the auxiliary flow is the heat flow.

For A,B1,B2∈ℝ2×2A,B_{1},B_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, define

ℰγ​(A,B1,B2)=∑i=12D2​fγ​(A)​[Bi,Bi].\mathcal{E}_{\gamma}(A;B_{1},B_{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{2}D^{2}f_{\gamma}(A)[B_{i},B_{i}].
Lemma 3.

Fix γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}. Suppose that

∫ℝ2ℰγ​(D​v,∂1D​v,∂2D​v)​𝑑x≥0\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mathcal{E}_{\gamma}\bigl(Dv;\partial_{1}Dv,\partial_{2}Dv\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x\geq 0 (2.1)

whenever v⁡(x)=F​x+ψ⁡(x)v(x)=Fx+\psi(x), with F∈ℝ2×2F\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} and ψ\psi in the Schwartz class. Then fγf_{\gamma} is quasiconvex.

Proof.

Fix F∈ℝ2×2F\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} and φ∈Cc∞​(ℝ2,ℝ2)\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{2}). Let

φτ=eτ​Δ​φ,Gτ=D​φτ,Aτ=F+Gτ.\varphi_{\tau}=e^{\tau\Delta}\varphi,\qquad G_{\tau}=D\varphi_{\tau},\qquad A_{\tau}=F+G_{\tau}.

Define

ℱ⁡(τ)=∫ℝ2[fγ​(Aτ)−fγ​(F)−tr⁡(D​fγ​(F)​GτT)],𝑑x.\mathcal{F}(\tau)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\bigl[f_{\gamma}(A_{\tau})-f_{\gamma}(F)-\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Df_{\gamma}(F)G_{\tau}^{T}\bigr)\bigr],\mathrm{d}x.

For τ>0\tau>0, integration by parts and ∂τAτ=Δ​Aτ\partial_{\tau}A_{\tau}=\Delta A_{\tau} give

ℱ′(τ)=−∫ℝ2ℰγ(Aτ;∂1Aτ,∂2Aτ)dx.\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(\tau)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mathcal{E}_{\gamma}\bigl(A_{\tau};\partial_{1}A_{\tau},\partial_{2}A_{\tau}\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x.

The hypothesis applied to vτ​(x)=F​x+φτ​(x)v_{\tau}(x)=Fx+\varphi_{\tau}(x) shows that ℱ\mathcal{F} is nonincreasing. The heat kernel estimate in two dimensions gives

∥Gτ∥Lp≤Cpτ−(1−1/p)∥Dφ∥L1,p=2,3,4.\|G_{\tau}\|_{L^{p}}\leq C_{p}\tau^{-(1-1/p)}\|D\varphi\|_{L^{1}},\qquad p=2,3,4. (2.2)

Since fγf_{\gamma} is quartic,

|fγ​(F+G)−fγ​(F)−tr⁡(D​fγ​(F)​GT)|≤Cγ​(|F|2​|G|2+|F|​|G|3+|G|4).\displaystyle\bigl|f_{\gamma}(F+G)-f_{\gamma}(F)-\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Df_{\gamma}(F)G^{T}\bigr)\bigr|\leq C_{\gamma}\bigl(|F|^{2}|G|^{2}+|F||G|^{3}+|G|^{4}\bigr). (2.3)

Equations (2.2) and (2.3) imply that ℱ⁡(τ)→0\mathcal{F}(\tau)\to 0 as τ→∞\tau\to\infty.

To justify the limit at zero, put

ℛF​(G)=fγ​(F+G)−fγ​(F)−tr⁡(D​fγ​(F)​GT).\mathcal{R}_{F}(G)=f_{\gamma}(F+G)-f_{\gamma}(F)-\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Df_{\gamma}(F)G^{T}\bigr).

Since ℛF\mathcal{R}_{F} is the sum of terms of degrees two, three, and four in GG,

|ℛF(G)−ℛF(H)|≤Cγ[\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{F}(G)-\mathcal{R}_{F}(H)|\leq C_{\gamma}\bigl[ |F|2​(|G|+|H|)+|F|​(|G|2+|H|2)\displaystyle|F|^{2}(|G|+|H|)+|F|(|G|^{2}+|H|^{2})
+|G|3+|H|3]|G−H|.\displaystyle+|G|^{3}+|H|^{3}\bigr]|G-H|.

Writing G0=D​φG_{0}=D\varphi and applying Hölder’s inequality gives

|ℱ(τ)−ℱ(0)|≤Cγ[\displaystyle|\mathcal{F}(\tau)-\mathcal{F}(0)|\leq C_{\gamma}\bigl[ |F|2​(‖Gτ‖L2+‖G0‖L2)​‖Gτ−G0‖L2\displaystyle|F|^{2}(\|G_{\tau}\|_{L^{2}}+\|G_{0}\|_{L^{2}})\|G_{\tau}-G_{0}\|_{L^{2}}
+|F|(‖Gτ‖L32+‖G0‖L32)​‖Gτ−G0‖L3\displaystyle+|F|(\|G_{\tau}\|_{L^{3}}^{2}+\|G_{0}\|_{L^{3}}^{2})\|G_{\tau}-G_{0}\|_{L^{3}}
+(∥Gτ∥L43+∥G0∥L43)∥Gτ−G0∥L4].\displaystyle+(\|G_{\tau}\|_{L^{4}}^{3}+\|G_{0}\|_{L^{4}}^{3})\|G_{\tau}-G_{0}\|_{L^{4}}\bigr]. (2.4)

For p=2,3,4p=2,3,4, strong continuity of the heat semigroup gives

‖Gτ−G0‖Lp=‖eτ​Δ​G0−G0‖Lp⟶0(τ→0).\|G_{\tau}-G_{0}\|_{L^{p}}=\|e^{\tau\Delta}G_{0}-G_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\longrightarrow 0\qquad(\tau\to 0).

The remaining norms in (2.4) are bounded for small τ\tau. Hence ℱ⁡(τ)→ℱ⁡(0)\mathcal{F}(\tau)\to\mathcal{F}(0) as τ→0\tau\to 0. Monotonicity therefore implies ℱ⁡(0)≥0\mathcal{F}(0)\geq 0. Since ∫ℝ2D​φ​𝑑x=0\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}D\varphi\,\mathrm{d}x=0, this is

∫ℝ2[fγ​(F+D​φ)−fγ​(F)]​𝑑x≥0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\bigl[f_{\gamma}(F+D\varphi)-f_{\gamma}(F)\bigr]\mathrm{d}x\geq 0.

For φ∈W01,∞​(Ω,ℝ2)\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_{0}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{2}), choose φj∈Cc∞​(Ω,ℝ2)\varphi_{j}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{2}) converging to φ\varphi in W1,4W^{1,4}. The estimate

|fγ​(F+G)−fγ​(F+H)|≤Cγ​(|F|+|G|+|H|)3​|G−H||f_{\gamma}(F+G)-f_{\gamma}(F+H)|\leq C_{\gamma}(|F|+|G|+|H|)^{3}|G-H|

and Hölder’s inequality allow passage to the limit. This proves (1.1). ∎

3 The correction lemma

Let α\alpha be a polynomial one-form on ℝ2×2\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, and let ω=d​α\omega=\mathrm{d}\alpha. If v⁡(x)=F​x+ψ⁡(x)v(x)=Fx+\psi(x), where ψ\psi is in the Schwartz class, then

(D​v)∗​ω=d⁡((D​v)∗​α).(Dv)^{*}\omega=\mathrm{d}\bigl((Dv)^{*}\alpha\bigr).

Every coefficient of (D​v)∗​α(Dv)^{*}\alpha contains a derivative of D​vDv, so this one-form is rapidly decreasing. Stokes’ theorem gives

∫ℝ2ωD​v​(∂1D​v,∂2D​v)​𝑑x=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega_{Dv}\bigl(\partial_{1}Dv,\partial_{2}Dv\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x=0. (3.1)

Fix |γ|≤2/3|\gamma|\leq 2/\sqrt{3}. To prove the sufficiency assertion in Theorem 1, Lemma 3 shows that it is enough to prove (2.1). In general, its integrand ℰγ​(D​v,∂1D​v,∂2D​v)\mathcal{E}_{\gamma}(Dv;\partial_{1}Dv,\partial_{2}Dv) is not pointwise nonnegative. We therefore seek an exact two-form ωγ\omega_{\gamma} whose addition makes this expression pointwise nonnegative. If this form has a polynomial primitive, its integral vanishes by (3.1). Integrating the corrected inequality then gives (2.1), and Lemma 3 proves quasiconvexity.

Lemma 4.

If |γ|≤2/3|\gamma|\leq 2/\sqrt{3}, there is an exact two-form ωγ\omega_{\gamma} on ℝ2×2\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, with homogeneous quadratic coefficients and invariant under

A⟼O​A​UT,O,U∈S​O​(2),A\longmapsto OAU^{T},\qquad O,U\in SO(2),

such that

ℰγ​(D​v,∂1D​v,∂2D​v)+(ωγ)D​v​(∂1D​v,∂2D​v)≥0\mathcal{E}_{\gamma}(Dv;\partial_{1}Dv,\partial_{2}Dv)+(\omega_{\gamma})_{Dv}(\partial_{1}Dv,\partial_{2}Dv)\geq 0

for every v∈C2​(Ω,ℝ2)v\in C^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{2}).

Proof.

It is enough to check this property for γ=2/3\gamma=2/\sqrt{3}, and we are going to reduce to this case throughout the proof.

Step 1. The function fγf_{\gamma} is invariant under rotations on the left and on the right. We impose the same invariance on the correcting form. Since the correction must be exact, we write ω=d​α\omega=\mathrm{d}\alpha and seek an invariant one-form α\alpha. The coefficients of ℰγ\mathcal{E}_{\gamma} are homogeneous of degree two in its first matrix argument. Thus ω\omega must have homogeneous quadratic coefficients, and α\alpha must have homogeneous cubic coefficients.

Write A=(𝐚1∣𝐚2)A=(\mathbf{a}_{1}\mid\mathbf{a}_{2}) and B=(𝐛1∣𝐛2)B=(\mathbf{b}_{1}\mid\mathbf{b}_{2}). For vectors in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, set 𝐚×𝐛=a1​b2−a2​b1\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1}. Two invariant linear one-forms are

θA​(B)\displaystyle\theta_{A}(B) =𝐚1×𝐛1+𝐚2×𝐛2,\displaystyle=\mathbf{a}_{1}\times\mathbf{b}_{1}+\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\mathbf{b}_{2}, (3.2)
ζA​(B)\displaystyle\zeta_{A}(B) =𝐚1⋅𝐛2−𝐚2⋅𝐛1.\displaystyle=\mathbf{a}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{b}_{2}-\mathbf{a}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{b}_{1}. (3.3)

Let J=(0−110).J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}. Then

θA​(B)=tr⁡(J​A​BT),ζA​(B)=tr⁡(A​JT​BT).\theta_{A}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(JAB^{T}),\qquad\zeta_{A}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(AJ^{T}B^{T}).

The one-forms in (3.2)–(3.3) have linear coefficients in AA. To make α\alpha homogeneous of degree three, we multiply them by the quadratic scalar quantities already present in the definition of fγf_{\gamma}, namely |A|2|A|^{2} and detA\det A. We use the four-parameter ansatz

α=c1​|A|2​θ+c2​(detA)​ζ+c3​|A|2​ζ+c4​(detA)​θ,ω=d​α,\alpha=c_{1}|A|^{2}\theta+c_{2}(\det A)\zeta+c_{3}|A|^{2}\zeta+c_{4}(\det A)\theta,\qquad\omega=\mathrm{d}\alpha, (3.4)

where c1,c2,c3,c4∈ℝc_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}\in\mathbb{R}.

In terms of the entries of AA,

θ\displaystyle\theta =A11​d​A21−A21​d​A11+A12​d​A22−A22​d​A12,\displaystyle=A_{11}\,\mathrm{d}A_{21}-A_{21}\,\mathrm{d}A_{11}+A_{12}\,\mathrm{d}A_{22}-A_{22}\,\mathrm{d}A_{12}, (3.5)
ζ\displaystyle\zeta =A11​d​A12−A12​d​A11+A21​d​A22−A22​d​A21.\displaystyle=A_{11}\,\mathrm{d}A_{12}-A_{12}\,\mathrm{d}A_{11}+A_{21}\,\mathrm{d}A_{22}-A_{22}\,\mathrm{d}A_{21}. (3.6)

Every rotation commutes with JJ, since JJ itself is a rotation. If T⁡(A)=O​A​UTT(A)=OAU^{T}, with O,U∈S​O​(2)O,U\in SO(2), then

(T∗​θ)A​(B)\displaystyle(T^{*}\theta)_{A}(B) =tr⁡(J​O​A​UT​(O​B​UT)T)=tr⁡(J​A​BT),\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(JOAU^{T}(OBU^{T})^{T}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(JAB^{T}),
(T∗​ζ)A​(B)\displaystyle(T^{*}\zeta)_{A}(B) =tr⁡(O​A​UT​JT​(O​B​UT)T)=tr⁡(A​JT​BT).\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(OAU^{T}J^{T}(OBU^{T})^{T}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(AJ^{T}B^{T}).

The functions |A|2|A|^{2} and detA\det A are invariant as well. Consequently, α\alpha and ω\omega in (3.4) are invariant under left and right multiplication. The form ω\omega is exact and has homogeneous quadratic coefficients.

Appendix A The invariant quartic cone

In this appendix we briefly record how the argument for the Dacorogna–Marcellini family extends to prove Theorem 2. Set

s⁡(F)=|F|2,d⁡(F)=detF.s(F)=|F|^{2},\qquad d(F)=\det F.
Proof of Theorem 2.

Invariant representation. We first show that every homogeneous quartic polynomial satisfying the invariance assumption in Theorem 2 has a unique representation of the form

Q⁡(F)=a​s​(F)2+b​s​(F)​d​(F)+c​d​(F)2.Q(F)=as(F)^{2}+bs(F)d(F)+cd(F)^{2}. (A.1)

Let

q⁡(x,y)=Q⁡(diag⁡(x,y)).q(x,y)=Q(\operatorname{diag}(x,y)).

Since QQ is homogeneous of degree four, qq is a homogeneous quartic polynomial in xx and yy. Moreover, with

J=(0−110),J​diag⁡(x,y)​JT=diag⁡(y,x),J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad J\operatorname{diag}(x,y)J^{T}=\operatorname{diag}(y,x),

and hence the rotational invariance of QQ gives q⁡(x,y)=q⁡(y,x)q(x,y)=q(y,x). Every symmetric homogeneous quartic in two variables has the form

q⁡(x,y)=A⁡(x4+y4)+B⁡(x3​y+x​y3)+C​x2​y2.q(x,y)=A(x^{4}+y^{4})+B(x^{3}y+xy^{3})+Cx^{2}y^{2}.

On diagonal matrices, s=x2+y2s=x^{2}+y^{2} and d=x​yd=xy, so

x4+y4=s2−2​d2,x3​y+x​y3=s​d,x2​y2=d2.x^{4}+y^{4}=s^{2}-2d^{2},\qquad x^{3}y+xy^{3}=sd,\qquad x^{2}y^{2}=d^{2}.

Thus (A.1) holds on every diagonal matrix. Every matrix F∈ℝ2×2F\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} can be brought to a signed diagonal matrix by proper rotations on the left and right. Since both sides of (A.1) are invariant under these rotations, the identity holds for every FF. Finally, s2,s​d,d2s^{2},sd,d^{2} are linearly independent already on diagonal matrices, which proves uniqueness.

Rank-one convexity. We next determine rank-one convexity. By the rotational invariance it is enough to test the direction

E11=(1000).E_{11}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}.

For A=(xyzw)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{smallmatrix}\right), direct differentiation gives

D2​Q​(A)​[E11,E11]=12​a​x2+6​b​x​w+(4​a+2​c)​w2+4​a​(y2+z2)−2​b​y​z.D^{2}Q(A)[E_{11},E_{11}]=12ax^{2}+6bxw+(4a+2c)w^{2}+4a(y^{2}+z^{2})-2byz.

Thus this expression is nonnegative for every AA if and only if

(12​a3​b3​b4​a+2​c)≥0,(4​a−b−b4​a)≥0.\begin{pmatrix}12a&3b\\ 3b&4a+2c\end{pmatrix}\geq 0,\qquad\begin{pmatrix}4a&-b\\ -b&4a\end{pmatrix}\geq 0.

Equivalently, either

a>0,|b|≤4​a,c≥−2​a+3​b28​a,a>0,\qquad|b|\leq 4a,\qquad c\geq-2a+\frac{3b^{2}}{8a}, (A.2)

or a=b=0a=b=0 and c≥0c\geq 0. By the Legendre–Hadamard characterization (1.2), these conditions describe the full rank-one convex cone.

Reduction to the boundary family. It remains to prove sufficiency for quasiconvexity. Suppose first that a>0a>0, and set

t=b4​a,μ=c+2​a−3​b28​a.t=\frac{b}{4a},\qquad\mu=c+2a-\frac{3b^{2}}{8a}.

Condition (A.2) says that |t|≤1|t|\leq 1 and μ≥0\mu\geq 0, and gives the decomposition

Q=a​Wt+μ​d2,Wt=s2+4​t​s​d+(6​t2−2)​d2.Q=aW_{t}+\mu d^{2},\qquad W_{t}=s^{2}+4tsd+(6t^{2}-2)d^{2}. (A.3)

The term d2d^{2} is polyconvex, hence quasiconvex. We only have to consider WtW_{t}.

Quasiconvexity of the boundary family. We use the invariant one-forms θ\theta and ζ\zeta defined in (3.2)–(3.3). Define the cubic one-form and its exact differential by

αt\displaystyle\alpha_{t} =[−3​t​s+6​(1−2​t2)​d]​θ+[3​s+6​t​d]​ζ,\displaystyle=[-3ts+6(1-2t^{2})d]\theta+[3s+6td]\zeta, (A.4)
ωt\displaystyle\omega_{t} =d​αt.\displaystyle=\mathrm{d}\alpha_{t}.

Both αt\alpha_{t} and ωt\omega_{t} are invariant under proper rotations on the left and right.

By the same argument used in Step 3 of the proof of Lemma 4, it suffices to take A=Aρ=diag⁡(1,ρ)A=A_{\rho}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\rho). At the point under consideration, write the derivative matrices as in the main proof:

B1=(ξ1ξ2η1η2),B2=(ξ2ξ3η2η3).B_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}\xi_{1}&\xi_{2}\\ \eta_{1}&\eta_{2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}\xi_{2}&\xi_{3}\\ \eta_{2}&\eta_{3}\end{pmatrix}.

Put

L=1+t​ρ,M=t+ρ,δ=1−t2.L=1+t\rho,\qquad M=t+\rho,\qquad\delta=1-t^{2}.

Differentiating WtW_{t} and (A.4), and collecting squares, gives

D2​Wt​(Aρ)​[B1,B1]+D2​Wt​(Aρ)​[B2,B2]+(ωt)Aρ​(B1,B2)\displaystyle D^{2}W_{t}(A_{\rho})[B_{1},B_{1}]+D^{2}W_{t}(A_{\rho})[B_{2},B_{2}]+(\omega_{t})_{A_{\rho}}(B_{1},B_{2})
=3​(2​L​ξ1+L​ξ3+M​η2)2+(L​ξ3−M​η2)2+4​δ​(ρ​ξ3−η2)2\displaystyle={}3(2L\xi_{1}+L\xi_{3}+M\eta_{2})^{2}+(L\xi_{3}-M\eta_{2})^{2}+4\delta(\rho\xi_{3}-\eta_{2})^{2}
+3​(L​ξ2+M​η1+2​M​η3)2+(L​ξ2−M​η1)2+4​δ​(ρ​ξ2−η1)2.\displaystyle\quad+3(L\xi_{2}+M\eta_{1}+2M\eta_{3})^{2}+(L\xi_{2}-M\eta_{1})^{2}+4\delta(\rho\xi_{2}-\eta_{1})^{2}.

This is nonnegative because |t|≤1|t|\leq 1. The same covariance and homogeneity argument gives the corresponding inequality for every A∈ℝ2×2A\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}.

Now let v⁡(x)=F​x+ψ⁡(x)v(x)=Fx+\psi(x), with ψ\psi in the Schwartz class. Exactness and (3.1) imply

∫ℝ2(ωt)D​v​(∂1D​v,∂2D​v)​𝑑x=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\omega_{t})_{Dv}(\partial_{1}Dv,\partial_{2}Dv)\,\mathrm{d}x=0.

After integration, the pointwise inequality therefore yields

∫ℝ2∑j=12D2​Wt​(D​v)​[∂jD​v,∂jD​v],𝑑x≥0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{2}D^{2}W_{t}(Dv)[\partial_{j}Dv,\partial_{j}Dv],\mathrm{d}x\geq 0.

The proof of Lemma 3 uses only that the integrand is a homogeneous quartic, so it applies verbatim and shows that WtW_{t} is quasiconvex. Hence (A.3) is quasiconvex. In the remaining case a=b=0a=b=0, one has Q=c​d2Q=cd^{2} with c≥0c\geq 0, which was already covered above.
